Ohio hosts AWS us-east-2 cloud region. The City of New Albany own published materials, along with CoStar, DataCenterDynamics, Data Center Frontier, and local television and news outlets including 10TV and NBC4, document a series of AWS investment announcements in the area, including a 3.5 billion dollar, five building campus expansion, an earlier 7.8 billion dollar investment reported in 2023, and city and county economic development materials describing a combined multi billion dollar footprint that the City of New Albany credits with contributing 1.4 billion dollars to Licking County gross domestic product. New Albany city council approved a 30 year local tax abatement to support the continued buildout. Some buildings in this campus carry community assigned tracking codenames such as CMH50, CMH53, CMH56, CMH59, and CMH62, referencing the Columbus airport code, which data center trend tracking sites use to distinguish buildings from satellite imagery and permitting records, though these are not AWS own official building designations. AWS does not publish individual building addresses, capacities, or specifications, so this specific building construction date, square footage, and critical IT megawattage cannot be independently confirmed from any AWS owned source, even though the broader New Albany area campus and its economic impact are extensively documented in government and trade press.

profile.regional_context: Ohio hosts AWS's us-east-2 cloud region. AWS and the City of New Albany have publicly confirmed a series of expansions: a $3.5 billion, five building campus announcement, a further $7.8 billion investment reported in 2023 per Axios, and city and county economic development materials citing a combined multi-billion dollar footprint and a $1.4 billion contribution to Licking County GDP per the City of New Albany's own materials. A 30 year local tax abatement was approved by New Albany City Council to support the buildout.
profile.disclosure_policy: Confirmed directly on AWS own Global Infrastructure page (aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/): AWS does not publish specific street addresses or per-building technical specifications (square footage, power capacity in MW) for its data centers, as a matter of stated security and operational policy. AWS states each Region consists of a minimum of three isolated, physically separate Availability Zones, each with independent power, cooling, and physical security, but does not break this down to individual facility addresses. This session confirmed this disclosure policy directly rather than assuming it, and applies this finding to AWS records that otherwise have no facility specific address, square footage, planned capacity, or critical_it_mw on file. This is a company wide policy finding, not a statement that no such facility exists at this location.

reading.body:
This building is one of many in Amazon Web Services' Ohio data center campus centered on New Albany, which hosts the us-east-2 cloud region. AWS does not publish individual building capacities, addresses, or specifications as a stated policy, so the power draw of this specific facility cannot be independently confirmed from AWS sources. The broader campus has absorbed at least $11.3 billion in announced AWS investment and generated an estimated $1.4 billion contribution to Licking County GDP, supported by a 30-year local tax abatement approved by New Albany City Council.

One industry index describes the regional us-east-2 campus at approximately 500 MW operational capacity, though AWS itself has not confirmed this figure. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 500 MW across the entire Ohio region would represent roughly 12,500 racks, though this is an assumption applied to an unconfirmed third-party estimate and does not reflect AWS's actual workload mix or this facility's specific share. The state context shows Ohio has 76 mapped data center facilities with only 8 publishing power figures totaling 60.4 MW, meaning the vast majority of the state's capacity, including AWS's campus, remains undisclosed.

This facility's importance to AI scaling cannot be assessed from published specifications. Ohio ranks ninth nationally by disclosed data center capacity among the 50 states, but this ranking reflects only the 8 percent of mapped facilities that publish figures and excludes the AWS campus entirely. Without per-building disclosure, this building's role in the state's actual AI infrastructure remains invisible to grid planners and capacity forecasters.
